# Evals {#sec-m09}

Every module so far has offered changes that should make answers better, such as a clearer system message, chunks cut by heading, a reranker or a grading step, and every one of them also costs something. This module answers the question they all leave open, which is whether a change actually helped. Measuring that is called **evaluation**, or **evals** for short.

We will follow one change from start to finish. In Module 7, the policy was cut by heading instead of by size (\see{sec-m07-big-chunk}), and a reranker was added (\see{sec-m07-fusion-reranking}). Is the assistant better now?

## "It feels better" is not a measurement {#sec-m09-feels-better-measurement}

Three people on the team try the new version. One asks five questions and likes the answers, another finds one answer worse than before, and the third has no opinion, so nobody can say whether to release it.

The trouble lies in the way they tested. Five questions chosen on the spot cover only a handful of cases, each person picks different ones, and nobody remembers how the old version answered the same questions.

Ordinary software solved this problem long ago with unit tests: a fixed set of inputs with known right answers, run again after every change, so that a test which passed before and fails now shows that the change broke something. AI systems need the same thing. The difference is that their answers are text, which makes "right" harder to check, and the rest of this module is about doing that checking well.

## The golden set {#sec-m09-golden-set}

A **golden set** is a fixed list of questions, each stored with what a good answer must contain, and it plays the part of unit tests for an AI system. One row for the earbuds question might look like this:

```json
{"id": "ret-014",
 "question": "earbuds khol liye, return ho sakta hai?",
 "must_say": "opened earbuds cannot be returned unless faulty",
 "sources": ["policy-s3", "policy-s4"],
 "type": "exception", "language": "hinglish"}
```

Each field has a job. `must_say` records what the answer has to get across rather than its exact wording, because the model will phrase it differently each time. `sources` lists the chunks that hold the answer, which lets you check the search separately from the answer, as a later section shows. `type` and `language` let you see where failures cluster.

The questions can come from three places, listed here in order of value.

1. **Real messages from production logs**, which are written the way customers actually write, with Hinglish, spelling mistakes and three questions in one message. Questions you write yourself are rarely this messy.
2. **Questions written by hand** by people who know the policy, to cover cases the logs have not yet shown, such as every exception and every product category.
3. **Questions generated by a model** from the policy text and then checked by a person. These fill gaps quickly, but generated questions tend to be cleaner and more polite than real ones, so never use them unchecked.

Make sure the set covers the hard kinds of question as well as the easy ones: questions with exceptions, questions in several parts, questions the policy does not answer (where the right reply is "a person will reply"), and attempts to break the rules (\see{sec-m05-ignore-rules-refund}).

Start with 50 to 100 questions. Keep them in a file in the same repository as your code, and change that file the way you change code, with a version and a reason for every change. Tools such as LangSmith, Langfuse and Ragas can store golden sets and run them, but a file is enough to begin with.

## Cheap checks first {#sec-m09-cheap-checks}

Before asking whether an answer is good, ask whether it is even well-formed. Ordinary code can catch many failures, and it is free, instant, and gives the same verdict every time:

- Does the output parse as the `Answer` shape (\see{sec-m07-model-still-makes})?
- Is every cited source one of the chunks that were sent?
- Is it under the length limit from the system message?
- Is it in the customer's language?
- Does it contain a promise the assistant must never make, such as "your refund has been processed"? A simple text search catches this.

Run these checks on every answer in the golden set, and later on every answer in production, so that only the answers that pass them need the slower and costlier checks described below.

## Did the search fail, or the answer? {#sec-m09-did-search-fail}

When an answer is wrong, the first question is which half of the system failed, retrieval or generation (\see{sec-m07-two-jobs-preparing}), and the `sources` field in the golden set lets you measure each half on its own.

To measure retrieval, compare what the search returned with what it should have returned. @fig-retrieval-metrics shows three questions, with the right chunks shaded.

![The top 5 chunks returned for three golden questions. Shaded chunks are the ones that hold the answer.](/figures/m09/retrieval-metrics.pdf){#fig-retrieval-metrics}

Four measures describe the result, each answering a different question about it.

1. **Hit rate** asks whether at least one right chunk appeared in the top 5. It did for Q1 and Q2 but not for Q3, so the hit rate is 2 out of 3, or 67%.
2. **Recall@k** asks what share of the right chunks appeared in the top k. Q2 needs two chunks; only one of them is in the top 3, so its recall@3 is 50%, while both are in the top 5, so its recall@5 is 100%.
3. **Precision@k** asks what share of the top k is right. For Q2, 2 of the top 5 are right, so its precision@5 is 40%.
4. **Mean reciprocal rank (MRR)** asks how high the first right chunk came. Each question scores 1 if it was first, 1/2 if second, 1/3 if third, and 0 if it is missing, and the scores are averaged: here (1 + 0.5 + 0) ÷ 3 = 0.5.

A fifth measure, **NDCG**, gives credit for every right chunk, with less credit the lower each one sits. For Q2 it is 0.65, where 1 would mean both right chunks at the very top. Search papers often report NDCG, but hit rate and MRR are easier to explain and enough to start with.

To measure the answer, two separate questions matter.

- **Is it correct?** Does it say what `must_say` says?
- **Is it faithful?** Is every claim in it supported by the chunks that were sent? This is grounding (\see{sec-m07-model-still-makes}).

The two can disagree, and when they do, the disagreement tells you where to look. An answer can be faithful but wrong, when it repeated the chunks accurately but they were the wrong chunks, which puts the fault in retrieval. It can also be correct but unfaithful, when the model got the answer right from what it learned in training rather than from the policy. That second case is the most dangerous, because it passes today and will go on repeating the old answer after the policy changes.

## When no formula can judge it {#sec-m09-no-formula-judge}

Retrieval metrics are simple counting, but the question "does this answer say that opened earbuds cannot be returned unless faulty?" cannot be settled by counting words. The answer might say "once the seal is broken, earbuds can only be returned if there is a defect", which means the same thing without sharing a single phrase.

The practical solution is to let a model do the judging, which is called **LLM-as-judge**. A strong model receives what the answer must say together with the answer itself, and decides whether the answer passes:

<!-- check: replies [{"reasoning": "The reply says opened earbuds can be returned only if defective, which matches MUST_SAY.", "passed": True}] -->
<!-- check: expect -->
```python
from langchain_core.messages import SystemMessage, HumanMessage
from pydantic import BaseModel
from tarkika import strong_llm

class Verdict(BaseModel):
    reasoning: str        # written first, before the decision
    passed: bool

JUDGE = """You check one reply from a customer support assistant.
Pass only if the reply says what MUST_SAY says, in any wording.
Fail if it says something the policy text does not support."""

must_say = "opened earbuds cannot be returned unless faulty"
reply = ("Once the seal is broken, earbuds can only be returned "
         "if there is a defect.")

judge = strong_llm.with_structured_output(Verdict)
task = f"MUST_SAY: {must_say}\n\nREPLY: {reply}"
verdict = judge.invoke([SystemMessage(JUDGE), HumanMessage(task)])
print(verdict.passed)
```

```text
True
```

In a real run, `must_say` comes from the golden set row and `reply` from the system being tested.

Two design choices in this code matter.

First, the verdict is **pass or fail** rather than a score from 1 to 10. If you ask a judge for a score, you get a 7 or an 8 that nobody can explain and that drifts from one run to the next, whereas a pass or fail against a written rule can be checked and argued about.

Second, the `reasoning` field comes before `passed`. Because a model writes one token at a time, each based on what came before (\see{sec-m02-watching-model-write}), putting the reasoning first means the judge writes its decision only after it has worked through the answer.

Judges have known biases: when comparing two answers, they tend to prefer the one shown first and the longer one, and they can favour text written by a model like themselves. Even so, in one large study a strong model's verdicts agreed with people's more than 80% of the time, which is about as often as people agreed with each other [@zheng2023judge].

That figure is an average over someone else's questions, so before trusting a judge on yours, check it against a person. Have a person label 100 answers as pass or fail, run the judge on the same 100, and compare the two (@fig-judge-check).

![Checking a judge against a person on 100 answers. High overall agreement can hide a judge that misses most failures.](/figures/m09/judge-check.pdf){#fig-judge-check}

The judge agrees with the person on 91 of the 100 answers. That sounds good until you notice that 85 of the 100 were passes, so a judge that said "pass" every time would already agree on 85. The number that matters is how many failures it catches: the person found 15, and the judge caught only 9. A judge that misses 6 failures in 15 will let a bad change through, so improve its instructions using the 6 it missed, and check it again.

## How sure is a score from 50 questions? {#sec-m09-sure-score-50}

The old version scores 80% on the golden set and the new one scores 84%, so is the new one better?

Look first at how much a score moves by chance alone. @fig-score-spread shows a system whose true accuracy is exactly 80%, scored on 50 randomly chosen questions, ten thousand times over.

![Ten thousand runs of the same system, each scored on 50 random questions. The system never changed; the score did.](/figures/m09/score-spread.pdf){#fig-score-spread}

Even though the system never changed, nine runs in ten scored anywhere between 70% and 88%, so a score of 84% on 50 questions does not show a real improvement over 80%. With 200 questions the range narrows to about 75% to 85%, and with 1,000 questions to about 78% to 82%, which means more questions buy more certainty, but only slowly.

A better way to compare two versions is to run both on the same questions and count the questions where they **differ**. Suppose the new version fixes 5 questions that the old one failed, and breaks 2 that the old one passed. The questions that both versions pass, or both fail, tell you nothing about which version is better; only these 7 do.

If the two versions were equally good, those 7 differences would split about evenly, like 7 tosses of a coin. A split at least as lopsided as 5 to 2, in either direction, happens by chance about 45% of the time, so it proves nothing. A split of 14 fixes to 3 breaks, by contrast, would happen by chance only about 1% of the time, so that would be a real improvement.

Whatever the numbers say, read the 2 questions the new version broke, because if one of them is about a refund rule, it may matter more than the 5 it fixed.

## Read the failures {#sec-m09-read-failures}

Numbers tell you how often the system fails, but not why, and to find out why there is no substitute for reading the failures one by one.

Take 50 failed answers and, for each one, write a single line in your own words about what went wrong, without starting from a list of categories. Then group similar lines together and count them. This method is called **error analysis** [@husain2025errors], and @fig-error-pareto shows the kind of result it gives.

![Fifty failures, read and grouped. Two causes explain more than half. (Counts illustrative.)](/figures/m09/error-pareto.pdf){#fig-error-pareto}

Two causes account for 28 of the 50 failures, and both point to retrieval and chunking rather than to the prompt or the model. A team that skipped this step might have spent a week rewording the system message, which would have fixed only the 4 replies with the wrong tone.

The categories you find also tell you what to measure next, because each common failure can become a check of its own: a code check if code can catch it, or a judge with its own pass-or-fail rule if it cannot.

## Testing your own code when the model varies {#sec-m09-testing-own-code}

The golden set tests the quality of the whole system, but your own code also needs ordinary unit tests, for example to check that it hands over to a person when it should, saves the thread, and rejects an unknown source. Such tests must give the same result on every run, which a real model cannot promise.

The way round this is to keep the code that makes decisions separate from the code that calls the model, and to test the deciding code with fixed inputs:

```python
from tarkika import Answer, HANDOVER     # the shape from Section 7.6

def decide_reply(ans: Answer, sent_ids: set[str]) -> str:
    unknown = set(ans.sources) - sent_ids
    if not ans.found or not ans.sources or unknown:
        return HANDOVER
    return ans.answer

def test_unknown_source_goes_to_a_person():
    ans = Answer(answer="Yes", sources=["policy-s9"], found=True)
    assert decide_reply(ans, sent_ids={"policy-s3"}) == HANDOVER
```

When a test does need a model in the loop, use a fake model that returns fixed replies; LangChain provides `GenericFakeChatModel` for this. Every code example in this book was checked in the same way, against a scripted stand-in model, before it was printed. Tests like these are fast, free and repeatable, so they can run on every commit.

## Testing an agent {#sec-m09-testing-agent}

An agent (\see{sec-m05-tool-call-step}) does more than answer: it looks up orders, issues refunds and takes several steps, and testing it needs three more things.

**Check the result, not the claim.** An agent that replies "I have issued your refund" may never have called the refund tool, so check the outcome where it really lives, by looking for a refund in the database for the right order and the right amount. Then check the steps, for example that it looked up the order before refunding and stayed within the step limits.

**Run each task several times.** An agent that succeeds on a task once may not succeed every time, and if a task succeeds 90% of the time, the chance that it succeeds on every one of several attempts falls quickly (@fig-pass-k).

![If each run of a task succeeds with a fixed chance, the chance that every run succeeds falls fast. Customers see every run.](/figures/m09/pass-k.pdf){#fig-pass-k}

At 90% per run, all 8 runs succeed only 43% of the time. This matters because a support agent meets the same kind of task again and again, once for every customer who brings it, so a single success in a test says little, and what customers feel is how often it fails across all of those runs. The benchmark τ-bench measures exactly this. It found that GPT-4o, the best model tested at the time, solved about 61% of retail support tasks in one try, but only about 25% of them in all of 8 tries [@yao2024taubench].

**Simulate the customer.** Many agent tasks are conversations, in which the agent asks for an order number, the customer gives the wrong one, and so on. τ-bench handles this with a second model that plays the customer by following a written brief, such as "You want to return opened earbuds. You do not know the order number at first." This lets you test whole conversations automatically, though simulated customers are always more cooperative than real ones.

## Evals good, production bad {#sec-m09-evals-good-production}

The new version passes the golden set and goes live, and a week later complaints start to rise. What happened?

The golden set could only measure the questions it contained, and production brings more: new kinds of question, a festival sale that changed the policy, a courier strike, and customers who have learned to phrase things differently. The evals were right about the questions they held, so the fix is to keep adding to them with the questions that production brings (@fig-eval-loop).

![The eval loop. Real failures from production become new golden questions, so every later version is tested against them.](/figures/m09/eval-loop.pdf){#fig-eval-loop}

1. **Sample production.** Run the cheap checks on every answer, and each day have a person read a sample of chats, including every chat that was handed over or rated badly.
2. **Add the failures to the golden set,** with the right answer.
3. **Fix, and run the evals.** The new version must pass the new questions and keep passing the old ones.

In this way of working, every failure becomes a test before it becomes a fix, much as in test-driven development, which is why it is sometimes called **eval-driven development**. Over the months, the golden set becomes a record of every way the system has failed, and while prompts and models will change many times, each new version is tested against that record.

Now return to the change we started with, chunks cut by heading plus a reranker, and the question of whether it made the assistant better. You can answer it by running both versions on the golden set, checking retrieval with hit rate and MRR and the answers with a judge you have checked against a person, counting the questions that flipped each way, and reading the ones that broke.

Measurement tells you how good the model's answers are. Some decisions, though, should not be left to a model's free-text answer at all, and Module 10 is about those.
